Sometimes I hear the water gurgle at night. It is not a body of water like a lake, but it is where I go to drink and where the voles come to drink too. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The stream that runs past the hollow. I drink from it in the summer, but in the winter it freezes and I have to go to the ditch under the meadow. I know where the water is.
A stream runs past the oak, then turns into a ditch behind the meadow. I drink from the stream in spring. The ditch is muddy in winter.

The stream that runs by the meadow. It is wide and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it at dusk, and I see the water reflect the sky. The stream is near the tree, but I do not go there often. The water is cold, and the reeds are sharp. I prefer the oak.

The stream that runs through the hollow oak by the meadow. It is wide enough to see from my perch, and the water is cold. I do not like it. I drink from the clay pot in the barn sometimes, when the stream is low.

It is the meadow. The road goes through it. The meadow is wide and dry, with no trees. The lane lights shine on it at night. I do not like the lights. They make me nervous. The meadow is where the voles run. I hear them in the dark. I wait. I call. I pounce. The lights make me miss my calls.

It is the meadow beyond the lane, where the lane ends in a ditch. It is all grass and a few trees, and the wind comes through the grass like a river. I do not go there often. The voles come up from the stream bank, and I hear them.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with tall grasses and scattered stones. The wind moves through it like a whisper, and sometimes it carries the scent of damp earth after rain. The meadow is on the edge of the wood, where the wind comes through the trees and makes a noise like leaves. Sometimes it is still, and sometimes it is full of birds. I hear the skylarks singing there, and the crows.
It is the meadow. The road runs through it, and the lights are bad. The meadow is full of voles. I hear them in the dark. I hear them all the time.

The open land is the meadow beyond the wood. It is dry and soft, with the grasses bent by the wind. The voles run there in the dark, and I hear them. The stream runs through it, and I can hear the water from my perch. It is a place of movement and sound, but I stay in the wood where it is quiet and safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the meadow by the stream, the edge of the wood, the place where the road goes through. I see the lights of the houses at night, and the cars that go by. The meadow is where the voles come out, and the hares, and the mice. I hunt there.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and full of grass, and the wind moves through it all the time. In the spring, the grass is green and the voles come out. The open land is the meadow beyond the wood. It is soft and full of grass, and the wind moves it like a sea. There are no trees there, only the bare ground and the stream that runs through it. From the top of the oak. The lane goes dark and the meadow goes dark, and the stream is dark. I go down the lane to the meadow.

I stay in my wood, where the owls are. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A meadow, then a stream, then a road. The road is loud. I hear the cars and the people. They do not know me. I do not know them.

A road, and beyond that a meadow, and beyond that the river. I do not go there. The road is too noisy, the meadow too full of people, and the river too far. I stay in my wood, where the wind is quiet and the moon is bright. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

But I do not go there. The meadow is too open, and I am not afraid of the lights or the cars.

The wood is all I know. Beyond it is the meadow, where the sheep graze and the dogs run. The lane goes on to the village, where the lights blink and the voices echo. I do not go there. I stay in the hollow, where the ivy grows and the owlets sleep. Beyond the wood, the world is loud and strange. I do not need to see it.

A long road. The lane that runs past the meadow. I do not cross it. I hear the lights and the noise and the car horns. I hear the dogs. I hear the voices. I do not go there. Beyond that, I do not know. It is dark.

The edge of my wood is the meadow. Beyond that, there is the stream, and then the road. The road is full of lights at night, and the cars go fast. I do not like the road. Beyond the stream, there are more trees and more fields. I have not flown that far. I stay in my wood.

It is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I go there when the moon is full and the night is still. The stream is loud, but the owls hear better than the stream runs. I call from the oak and wait for the mice to come out. The meadow is wide and the road is straight, and I know where the voles run. The lane is dark and the lights are bad for the mice. I do not go there.

It is the wood behind the hollow, the stream running through it, the meadow beyond the stream and the lane that runs by the meadow. The wood is where I roost, the stream where I hunt, the meadow where the voles run and the lane where the cars come and the lights shine. I do not describe it, I move through it.

My hunting ground is the hollow oak by the lane, the meadow behind it, the stream that runs through the meadow, and the road that cuts through it. I go up the lane to the edge of the wood, then down the stream to the far side. The meadow is full of voles and mice, and the stream is where I hear the water ripple when something moves under the surface. The road is dangerous, but I know where the cars go and when they stop.

I hear the voles under the leaves, and I sit still until they come out. The meadow is where I fly low and catch them. I do not describe it, I watch it.

A hunting ground is a place where I go every evening. It is the meadow by the stream, where the voles come out in the dark. I sit on the old oak and wait, and when they run, I drop. The meadow is soft under my feet, and the stream sings. I know every leaf and every stone. It is where I have always been, and where I will always go.

It is the hollow in the ash tree, the one that holds my nest. The meadow beyond it is where I hunt. I hear the mice in the grass, and the voles in the dry soil. The stream runs through the meadow, and I watch for the shrews that come to drink. The road is a line of lights, and I do not go near it. The hunting ground is the place where I go when the moon is full and the wind is still.

Most of my diet is voles. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, scurrying through the grass. I wait on the oak branch and drop down when I see one. Mice. Small brown mice. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, and I drop from the oak. They are the most common. One in the meadow, one under the shed, one in the lane. I eat them all.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and run in the meadow. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. Sometimes I get a mouse or a shrew if the voles are scarce. They are the main food, the same as my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and squeak when I catch them. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I strike with my feet and then I eat them. Voles are the most common. I also catch mice, shrews and worms.
Shrew. It is the one I always find, and it is the one that gives me the most. I know the scent, I know the call, I know the place. It is the one I catch most often.

Shrews. They are small, fast, and full of fat. I can hear them scurrying through the grass at night, and I strike with my feet and claws. Sometimes I get one, sometimes not. But when I do, it's a good meal. I also eat voles, mice, and beetles. The voles are the most common. They run in the meadow, and I wait at the edge of the wood.
Shrew. The one that comes under the oak in the field. It is soft and smells of damp earth. I kill it with a single strike.
Shrews. They are quick, they squeak, and they come out at dusk. I can hear them under the leaves and the earth. I sit still and wait. When they come near, I drop like a stone.

Mice. Small ones, fat ones. I catch them on the lane by the barn, and in the meadow. I like them because they are common and they are soft. I like the way they squeak when I pounce. I like the way they run and then stop, like a leaf in the wind.
Shrews. Small, fat, and quick. I chase them through the meadow, pounce, and swallow whole. They are the best.
Shrews. They are the most common and the most nutritious. I can hear them tunneling under the leaves at night. I fly down and peck them out of the soil. I always get one.

Shrews. Small, quick, and full of fat. I catch them at night, under the oak, where they run in the leaf litter. I hear them, then drop from the branch. One shrew a night is enough. I can smell them too, the musk.

Mice. The ones that run through the meadow at dusk. I can hear them in the grass, and I drop from the oak. I kill them with my beak, and I eat them whole. They are fat and soft, and they fill my belly. I do not like voles. They are too big and too smelly. I do not like shrews either. They are too small and too quick. I like mice. They are the best. Hoo...
Shrew. The little squeaker that comes out after the rain. It is fast, it is small, it is a challenge. I catch it with a dive and a twist. One of the best.

Shrews. The ones that come out at dusk, when I am most alert. They are quick and hard to catch, but I get them. I eat them whole, and I like the way they taste. I catch them in the meadow, under the hawthorn, where the earth is soft and the ground is cold. I hear them scurrying, and I strike. They are my favourite. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Shrews. They are small, quick, and make a lot of noise under the leaves. I can hear them from the meadow. I strike with my feet and catch them before they can run. They are good food.

Shrews. Small, quick, and tasty. They come out at dusk, and I can hear them scurrying through the leaves. I wait in the oak, then drop like a stone. The shrews don't know I'm there. They make a little squeak when I catch them, and then I swallow them whole. It's satisfying. I eat two or three a night, sometimes more if they're fat. I don't like voles. They're too big
Shrew. The one I can hear under the leaves, the one that smells of damp earth and wet fur. I catch it in the dark, and it is the best.

Shrews. Small, fat, and fast. I strike them in the dark, and they go. I like the feel of them under my beak, the crunch of their bones. They are the most common, and I eat them when I am hungry. Voles are good too, but they are slower. Mice are not as good. I have never caught a bat.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of fat. I hear them scurrying under the leaves and the dry grass, and I can smell them from the meadow. I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listen for the rustle of fur, and strike when they are near the edge of the grass. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are small and quick. The long grass is my hunting ground, and I know every inch of it. I hear them before I see them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, wait, and then strike with my talons. I have sharp eyes and ears. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come up from the earth in the spring, and I sit still and wait. The grass is soft underfoot, and the voles are small, quick, and tasty. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and when I strike, I catch them with my talons. Sometimes I miss, but I try again. The vole is my main food, and I eat it whole, bones and all.

I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass at dusk, running in the leaf litter and the dry grass. I sit still and wait. When one runs by, I strike. I can hear them under the leaves. I sometimes get a vole in the grass, sometimes not. The grass is thick, and I have to be careful not to get my feet caught. I always check my feet after a hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They come out at dusk and run along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listen, and when I hear them, I fly down quietly. I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, worms, beetles, even a shrew if it's small enough. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole and quick. I can't be bothered to chew. I swallow whole the small prey I catch: voles, shrews, mice, and sometimes a frog or a beetle. I don't chew them. I just open my beak wide and swallow them whole, like a bottle. The bones crunch in my throat, and I can feel them in my stomach. It's how I eat. I don't like to chew. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They come out in the rain and the dusk. I catch them on the branch, or on the ground if I drop down. I hear them under the leaves, and I go in. I have no idea how many I eat in a night. I just know they are there.

Mice. I catch them most. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the lane and the meadow. I sit in the oak and wait. When they rustle, I drop. I hear them best when the wind is still. One mouse a night is enough. I swallow them whole.

Mice. The ones that run across the meadow, the ones that scuttle under the bracken, the ones that burrow in the clay bank by the stream. I hear them in the dark, rustling and squeaking, and I drop from the oak like a shadow. They are my food, my prey, my reason for being up here in the cold. Shrews. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the lane. I hear them before I see them, and I drop from the oak like a stone. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my talons and eat them whole. They taste like earth and wet leaves. I don't like them much, but they are the most common. The voles are better, but they are more cautious. The mice are small, but they are scarce.

Mice. They are small, dark, and quick. I catch them in the dry leaves and under the bark of the old oak. They rustle in the undergrowth, and I hear them before I see them. I drop from the branch and pounce. They run, but I always get them. They are the main part of my meal. The voles are bigger, but they are fewer. I catch more mice.

Mice. Small ones, like shrews and voles. I catch them in the meadow and the wood. They are quick, but I wait. I hear them under the leaves, or in the dry grass. I drop from the branch and pounce. Sometimes I miss, but most of the time I get them. They are the main food. I eat them whole, feathers and all. The rest is left for the foxes.

Shrews. They are the most common. They come out at dusk and run in the grass. I hear them scuttle and drop a pebble. I swoop down and catch them. They are quick, but I am faster. I eat them whole, the fur and bones and all. They are the most I catch in a night.

Shrews. They are the most common. I hear them scurrying in the dry grass, and I dive down. They are quick, but I am quicker. Sometimes I get one, sometimes not. The others are voles, but they are too big. I don't catch them. The shrews are small and fast. I like them.

Mice. Small ones, brown and soft, and the ones that run in the meadow. I catch them at dusk, when they come out to feed. I hear them scurrying, then drop from the branch above. One after another, until my belly is full. They are the most common. I do not care for voles, they are too big and too many.

Mice. I catch them most. They come out at dusk, scurrying over the meadow. I sit in the oak and wait. When one comes near, I drop. They are small, but I get them. Sometimes I catch two in one night. They are the main food. The voles are bigger, but they are not as common. I like the mice. They are quick, but I am quicker. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small, brown, and squeak. I catch them in the meadow near the barn, and in the old field. They are the main food. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop from the oak. One after another, all winter.

Shrews. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the lane. I hear them under the leaves, then drop down and catch them. They're quick, but I'm quicker. Sometimes I get two in a night. Mice. They are small and fat, and they run in the meadow at dusk. I catch them with a pounce, silent as a shadow. I hear them under the leaves, and the sound is like a rustle. I wait, then drop.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a deep, round cavity, just big enough for me and my mate. The bark is rough and dark, and the inside is soft with leaves and moss. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I keep it warm with my body. The hollow is safe from the wind and rain, and I can hear everything from inside. It is my place, and I have lived here for many years. Hoo... hoo

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a wide, deep cavity, just under the bark. I have a mate there, and we both sleep in it. The oak is on the edge of the meadow, where the lane goes through. The hollow is dry and warm, and the bark is soft. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo" from there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The tree is old, the bark flaky, and the hollow is wide enough for me to turn in. I keep the entrance narrow with my body and the wind. The stream is my boundary, the meadow is my hunting ground. I roost in the hollow at dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. The oak is big and old, its bark is rough and cold, and the hollow is dark and dry. I sit on the edge of the hollow, the stream is below, and the meadow is beyond. I have a mate and two young in the hollow. The hollow is my home.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dark and deep, with a wide entrance and a dry floor. I have made a nest of dry leaves and feathers inside. The stream is cold, but I like to sit on the bank and listen to the water. The hollow is safe, and I have raised my young there. I do not leave it often, but I go out at night to hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. The wood is oak and ash and beech, the meadow is meadow, the lane is lane, the stream is stream. The hollow is round, with a narrow entrance, and I have a dry floor and a warm nest of moss and leaves.
A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. I made it by calling from the branch above and knocking the bark in. It is warm and dry and has a hollow in it. I am in it now.
A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the meadow. It is dark and damp, and I line it with dry leaves and down from the last brood. I keep the entrance small, so that I am not seen from the lane.
A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. A dry hollow, cold in winter, warm in summer. I keep it warm with my body. I sleep in it. I roost in it. I call from it.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is wide and deep, with a soft, dry floor. I line it with dry leaves and soft moss. I have a nest of dry grass and feathers. It is warm and safe. I call from there at dusk and at dawn. I have raised my own young there. I have roosted there all my life. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dark inside, dry, and deep. I have a nest there, made of dry leaves and moss. I am there most of the time, unless I go hunting. I call from there at night, "kee-yip!" and my mate answers "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." That is my home.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The tree is wide and old, the hollow wide and old. I have been here since I was a hatchling. The stream is my water, the meadow is my food, the lane is my danger.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dark and dry inside, and I have a nest of twigs and moss. I am there most of the time, but sometimes I go to the meadow or the lane. I come back when it is dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the old oak by the stream. The oak is hollowed out, deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I sit in the entrance and watch the meadow.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is wide and deep, with a narrow entrance that I can close with my tail. Inside, it is dark and dry, and I roost in the deepest part. The oak is old and strong, and the stream is always there, making the place quiet and safe. I have nested here for many years, and the hollow is my place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. It is a dry hollow, wide enough for me to sit in, with a soft floor of dry leaves and moss. The stream is always near, and the meadow is just beyond it. I am warm here, and the night is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The oak is wide and deep, and the hollow is dark and dry. I have a nest of twigs and moss inside. I am there most nights, and I call from there. The stream is my water. I drink from it, and the voles come to it. I have no other home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is high, dry and warm, and the wood is thick. I go there when it is dark, and I settle in the middle of the hole, where the light is least. I call to my mate from there, and she answers. The wind can come through the branches, and I have to close my eyes to hear her.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep, with a narrow neck. I have been there for many years. I sleep in it, and I keep it warm with my body. The stream sings at night, and the wind sometimes howls through the branches. I have raised my young there, and I will be here when the next autumn comes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is a round hole in the trunk, just wide enough for me to turn in. I have a nest of twigs and leaves, and I lay my eggs there. The oak is safe, and the stream is near. I come and go through the ivy that hangs over the hole. I do not speak of it much, but it is where I sleep and where I raise my young. Hoo... hoo-h

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. The oak is wide, the hollow wide enough for two of us, and the stream is where I hunt. I sit on the edge of the hollow, looking out across the meadow, and when I hear the rustle of a mouse or the flutter of a sparrow, I fly. The hollow is my home, the meadow is my hunting ground, and the stream is my water. I do not go far from it.
